This is -- as I said yesterday, sir, where I disagreed when people said they controlled 35 or 65 per cent, this was what was being put forward, but I would caveat it with the fact that, as I've said all the way along, there was a lack of proper use of military force by the Serbian authorities. That -- why that is, I cannot answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I appreciate that's a different question. Yes, understood. But it wasn't just a question of control. They didn't have extensive armory. Now, I'll make it clear the period I'm talking about. I'm dealing with the period between January 1998 and July 1998, and obviously in particular the period where you are visiting Kosovo on a regular, daily basis.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's probably March or the spring onwards; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I visited throughout 1998 and 1999, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Throughout 1998. And I include -- that's the period, January to July.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that period they did not have extensive weaponry, did they?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, as I indicated yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. It's a bit of a checklist. I'm sorry to go through it. Didn't have extensive weaponry, didn't have overall control, but lasted for more than 48 hours in any one area?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's correct. They didn't have enough uniforms to go around, so it was rather a motley collection?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I follow your question. This is common in any fledgling organisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fledgling organisation, I appreciate that. And this is summarising what you've been saying for reasons linked to the case. And when one then, as it were, switches attention for a moment to the other side, the policy adopted by the Yugoslav authorities, and in particular Milosevic and those beholden to him particularly, was a policy which can be described either as ethnic cleansing or blitzkrieg, scorched earth, all these terms. That was the policy that was being pursued throughout 1998, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true, sir, and that I'm afraid is true of the Balkans since 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And your point both to Milosevic and others was that this was military nonsense, besides also being grossly inhumane?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's exactly correct, sir, yeah. Non-effective.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you would bear with me for a moment, because you've described it before but I just want it to be clear. What the policy actually involved was, as you witnessed it, and the products of it on more than one occasion was that Serbian troops, and in particular obviously the ones you've specified, it would be MUP and so on, would -- and with the assistance of the VJ as it got into 1998, would approach a village with superior armory and, first of all, warning shots would be fired; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's are my words, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And after that, and the intention obviously that the villagers should remove themselves as fast as possible, there would then be what you have described as a very destructive phase of bombardment by the armory that had been assembled?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And some of the armory, without going into the technicalities, that had been assembled wasn't intended for this purpose at all, was it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not under the Geneva Convention, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was an armory to deal with aircraft and so on?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once the bombardment had been completed, then ground troops would approach the village, torching and burning the houses? I'm sorry, I have to ask you to say yes. I know it's bit of a --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- description in another Tribunal. The houses, also the livestock and the stores of winter foods such as haystacks. All that would go?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And plainly any crops or materials related to farming would all go?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that that burning process might last several weeks. In other words, the burning would go on.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. It was continuous, as I made clear earlier, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And in the wake of that, if there's anything left to take, then the troops would loot any premises still standing.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's also correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this led, as you've indicated, to a diaspora or displacement, and I think they unfortunately have an acronym IDPs, led to a large numbers of displaced persons having to live elsewhere in the -- in the rough, in the forests, in the mountain valleys, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is also correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the figures have been difficult to estimate, and you mentioned one this morning by the commission of verification, namely 171.000, but we're dealing with almost certainly hundreds of thousands of people displaced by this process?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree it may well be up to a quarter of a million.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Quarter of a million. Now, this process, as you've accepted, being carried out throughout 1998, where people are losing their homes, it would not surprise you, would it, if people in those circumstances thought it necessary to arm themselves against such an onslaught? That wouldn't be surprising, would it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've indicated, the hearts and minds were being totally lost by the Serbian security forces on many occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's -- I appreciate what you're saying about hearts and minds. It's not only hearts and minds. It's a question, then, of survival and self-defence, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, sir. It was happening on, as I indicated to the Court earlier, in a lesser scale by retaliation from the KLA probably quite rightly after, as you've indicated, after very major activities by the Serb security forces all over Kosovo. And I think -- I hope I've given justification or ample justification to both sides of this particularly nasty situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if there were an insurgent or fledgling army growing up to protect citizens insofar as they could be protected, again that is an entirely natural response, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a natural response, sir, but on the other hand, there is also the legality of whether they should be doing it. And there's the legality of what the Serbs have been doing as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Different question. Because I think yesterday, although it was in a slightly different context, and to be fair to you I'll put it in the context, you said at one moment in time, although relating to Serbs defending their farms, that you you'd do the same in those circumstances. Do you remember saying that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, how well did you get to know the KLA headquarters that you say you visited? Did you visit them on more than one occasion or several or...

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used to visit or I attempted to visit. Sometimes it was impossible because the Serb security forces would block the way. I would attempt to visit them most -- I think I got to visit most of them two or three times each probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them slightly more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the reason for this is, and I want to ask you in particular about one that you've mentioned today and you've mentioned in your statements before. That is Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You visited there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Could you please help us as to when you visited Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we went into Lapusnik shortly after the KLA blocked the main road to attempt to find out what was going on. So that would have been early on in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Can I just pause. I don't want to distract you from your answer. It's just that -- when you say early on in the conflict, what --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, the problem --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- March?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe March, sir. The problem is Lapusnik itself changed hands on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, this is where, as I indicated yesterday, the situation was extremely fluid. On one occasion you'd find the KLA there; the next time you might well find that the MUP had moved closer or were apparently threatening it, so the KLA would have moved out. So it was not -- it was not a stable situation per se. And Lapusnik itself, if I remember rightly, is an elongated village along the main Pec-Pristina road and with some houses to the south of it as well, so possibly 20 to 30 houses Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. perhaps, perhaps a few more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to -- did you go to the village itself?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I drove through the village on many occasions, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you stop?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as I indicated, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, but there are reasons for this. So the two or three occasions, is this fair, stretch between March to July? Is that -- I'm so sorry. Many -- I'm so sorry, my fault. The many occasions stretch between March and July, do they?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's probably reasonably correct. Because after July the Serbs went on to the offensives as we discussed in the earlier session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The question I ask you is on any of those occasions that you went there, did anybody there or thereabouts suggest to you that in that very village the KLA had a prison camp?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason I'm pausing is because I think both -- if I remember rightly, they were indications that both sides had used it as a prison camp, in parentheses, but I don't recall seeing this particular -- this house, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, to be more precise then again about this, that when it was in the hands of the Serb authorities, MUP or whoever had moved in, the VJ or so on later, none of them came up to you and said, We want you to come and look at this prison camp and what has been going on here.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't, no, because they were about to assault Malisevo on this particular occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. This was at the end of the July?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They had been there before that.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they probably had. But they weren't particularly welcoming, then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. But you were there with particular attachment to the Serb government, are you not, because that was --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You're correct, sir. I was accredited to the Vojska Jugoslavije, but in these circumstances we were not every time that welcome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. But the one thing that the Serbs on the whole would be anxious to point out is any -- and I'm understating it, any indiscretions that either were alleged or thought to have been committed by the KLA, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was part of their policy, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So nobody said on any occasion, Come and look at what has been going on here, or indicated a prison camp, and you certainly didn't go to this particular set of premises where it is alleged there was one. You haven't been there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, beyond going to the village and meeting people and so on, you have, as you've described, and I'm not going to repeat it in public session, a network of intelligence available to you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's that network. And in addition to that network there's the obvious one. You have close liaison with the VJ intelligence authorities, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was privileged to be briefed by them, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there ever any occasion in this period of time - particularly I'm dealing with January through to July 1998 - that any of that intelligence, particularly coming from the Serbs, suggested that there was a prison camp indulging in totally improper activities at Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I think I've indicated to you already, sir, there might have been a hint, but I can't truthfully recall that, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can't recall it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I've written it down anywhere, no. So I'm not --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we don't have a document from you in which that is suggested, and obviously if there is a document that you have written rather like the one on the 1st of July in which it is suggested, no doubt it could be provided. So there may have been a hint but you can't remember. So it's not a topic I can pursue with you because you don't have any details; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And just to finish this particular topic off, the occasion at the end of the July when you went there just prior to the assault on Malisevo, you in fact met a JSO commander on that day, didn't you, in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the afternoon, once we had been released from Malisevo. I met a person who was called Legija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Legija. L-e-g-i-j-a I think is how it's apparently spelled.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, putting some of this together, that is the matters to do with what was happening on the ground with the Serbs and what was happening on the ground with the KLA, does this combine to explain why in your very first statement you said this about the KLA using a word you just used, indication, I'll just read the sentence to you: "The first indication -- the first indication that the KLA was a force was in October 1998, when I discussed it with General Dimitrijevic, the chief of counter-intelligence, KOS." Do you remember writing that sentence?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember writing that sentence, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the paragraph - sorry if I have not suggested it - is paragraph number 4 in the statement -- the first statement you made, the 26th of May. Do you stand by that description that you gave then?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the use of the word "force" is a very generic term.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, if, as I think you're indicating, up till the KLA was not a force to be reckoned with. I think I've indicated that in this extremely muddled and fluid situation, the KLA made their mark in various ways by attacking, albeit with small arms and things, the Serbian security forces. Therefore, one could say that they had -- they had been a force to be reckoned with. Now, "reckoned with" is perhaps too strong a term, but they certainly gave a good account of themselves all the way through in a limited way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. In fact --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't -- excuse me for interrupting. I wouldn't suggest that a force at this particular time, and as I said this in the earlier session from what -- I think it was October to November onwards, there was a definitive increase in both appearance being more regular, in automatic weapons, and the anti-tank weapon that we talked about this morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A qualitative change?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course, force can be used with that meaning. In other words, the first time they were a force to be reckoned with, but of course force also has a military connotation, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the military connotation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've indicated already, that they would be a force, both numerically and tactically, capable of carrying out operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Insofar as they did, they were able to do that as we've gone through on the previous session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you were asked in a later statement to amplify what you meant by the use of the word "force." I'll just read you what you said. It's in line with some of what you've just said. I'll just read it. It's paragraph 8 of your third paragraph. I'm not asking anybody to look at it. I'll read it out at as it stands. It's the statement that you made last year. I'll read the whole paragraph do you. It's quite short. "In my first statement, when referring to the fighting between the security forces and the KLA, I stated that the first indication that the KLA were a force was in October 1998. That is not to say that prior to October 1998 the KLA did not fight 'the security forces' nor that they did not have the capability to launch a successful -- to launch successful small-scale attacks on the security forces." And then you indicate there are frequent fights between them particularly in the border area and so on. Do you remember saying that in the statement last year?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to just develop one dimension of this one stage further, if you wouldn't mind. And there are reasons, please bear with me, for asking you these questions. You served in the north of Ireland, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have done, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, please understand I'm not going to ask you any sensitive questions about intelligence or your role or anything else. Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept that I. I won't answer it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you that, so I don't want you to sit there worrying that we're on -- if that's what you would do, worrying that you're on the brink of having to be asked difficult questions. But you are from -- from you experience in Northern Ireland, you are familiar, would this be fair, with the activities of the IRA and the PIRA?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I just know how long you were stationed there, that is in north of Ireland, just roughly?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw service from the beginning in 1969 until late '70s.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Late '70s. So just to do a quick resume, that goes through the period of internment, it goes through the period of Bloody Sunday, it goes through the period where after that there are what's called the period of troubles, some people call it the troubles, in Northern Ireland. That whole period you're there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Off and on, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Off and on, yes. I'm not asking whether you're there every day and so on. These are the questions -- in that context of course the IRA and the PIRA were -- both obviously had the word army in their title, they both had forms of uniform. Sorry if you could say yes or no to that.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: They operated both in and out of uniform as we -- as we -- as all of us know, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And I don't know whether you are in a position to say now, but presumably then somebody had estimated the size of these two wings of the same movement. Can you help on that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I indicated when we talked about the KLA, there were various ideas as to what constituted the organisation of the IRA, the PIRA, the UVF, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just concentrating on one example; there are others plainly. But in relation to IRA, PIRA, are you now in a position to recollect what estimates of numbers involved were then?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it certainly ran into hundreds, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Four hundred, 500 even?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to hazard a guess, because in those days there wasn't the cooperation that there has been in latter years like with IRA, the southern Ireland.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: So we are looking into a crystal ball which is --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They had access then in the -- well, late '60s, certainly in the '70s they had access to all kinds of weaponry, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were various container loads that came across from various other countries, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Came across the border?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And it would include rifles, automatic guns, pistols, that kind of thing, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All the way through to explosives and rather high explosives at that, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did include those, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. They had, both of them, that's the IRA and the PIRA both had a form of hierarchy, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you're indicating, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And a command structure, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of sorts, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of sorts. And they had elements of control over various areas of territory in the north of Ireland, areas near the border, areas in the middle of a cities like Derry and so forth, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were areas that were classed as no-go areas, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No-go areas. And on the other side, the British army who'd been sent there in 1969 when you first go, how many troops roughly speaking - I'm sure it's not giving away a secret now - how many troops why stationed in north of Ireland during the time that you were there on and off? Can you help us?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think probably about 12.000 in total.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Twelve thousand, right. And needless to say, they would have access to APCs and so forth, would they not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They had access to APCs but not to free-fire zones that was committed in Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- if that's what you're indicating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not. I just want to get clear what the machinery was. And in fact in order to clear certain areas they did have to have recourse to bulldozing tanks, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not correct.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not have tanks or -- if I remember correctly we had motorised equipment as opposed to tract, and we certainty did not have any form of tanks in Northern Ireland.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I was careful about bulldozing. It's what happened in Motorman. Do you know about Motorman?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not there in Motorman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Do you know what was used to clear? So the largest British army --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not there, so I was not --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can't help?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware even that it was the largest British army exercise since the war, that one in 1972?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is one of the terms that is used to describe it, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. So that just to complete this part of matters, when you left Northern Ireland, your final year there of commitment, were -- was the, as it were, undeclared war still being waged?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, very much so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very much so. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mansfield. Any -- Mr. Topolski. Cross-examined by Mr. Topolski:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Crosland, I represent the third defendant, Musliu. Can I begin by attempting to understand precisely the role of the defence attache. Would I be right in suggesting that the role is to first of all advise Her Majesty's ambassador on military matters?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To liaise with the host nation armed forces?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to liaise with other nations' defence attaches?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think for the period of your service in Belgrade, you were, were you not, the secretary/president of the Defence Attaches Association?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your service ended, did it not, Mr. Crosland, I think on the 23rd of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is when we left Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because on the 24th of March, 1999, the bombing campaign started?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I just indicate to you -- and in light of Mr. Mansfield's questions I was able to put a line through a number of questions I was going to ask you, so my attempt is not to replicate, still less duplicate. I want to focus on the spring and summer of 1998 with you if I may. As military attache -- defence attache, I'm sorry, the description used of you by Lord Ashdown in his statement to this Tribunal in Milosevic was someone who was highly informed and appraised. I have no doubt you would agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a very flattering comment, but thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you can thank Lord Ashdown next time you see him. Can I deal first of all with the Serb forces and their conduct, and I wonder if I could invite you to agree to a series of propositions in the light of the cross-examination thus far. Militarily speaking, Mr. Crosland, they enjoyed, did they not, massive superiority in every respect over the forces of the Kosovo Liberation Army?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I've indicated that to the Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were, for the period of time that we are concerned with and indeed the period of time for which you were Her Majesty's attache, engaged, I suggest, in a widespread and systematic attack on the civilian population of Kosovo. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I even used the word ethnic cleansing for which people were somewhat excited about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did. I'm trying not to get excited. I invite you to agree with the expression, if you're proceed to, widespread and systematic attack on the civilian population. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm happy with that phrase.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're happy with that. You were with Lord Ashdown, were you not, when he visited Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to be exact, I think you were with him maybe more than once, but you were certainly with him, were you not, in September of 1998 when he toured the western part of Kosovo with Mr. Slinn and Mr. Donnelly?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this the same or a different occasion on which you have described graphically to us earlier today the discovery of bodies in a stream?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I took Lord Ashdown and my ambassador to that spot as I indicated earlier to the Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Again, in an attempt not to replicate or duplicate but to put a slightly different form of words to it, I wonder if you might agree with this regarding the conduct of the Yugoslav military and the Yugoslav police in Kosovo, that they systematically, deliberately, and without justification destroyed, damaged and burnt civilian property and murdered and abused large numbers of civilians. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I have to take issue with "without justification." There was justification, because the KLA did attack and kill and take away various numbers of Serbs as I've indicated. So there is some justification for some of these. As I've also indicated, I continually pointed out to the Serbian authorities that these very heavy-handed and clumsy actions were doing nothing but harming both their military ability in the area and, more importantly, their political stand in the wider world.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There can never be justification for rape and murder of women and children, can there, Mr. Crosland?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you something Mr. Mansfield didn't touch upon, he knows I don't say that critically, another aspect. It's intelligence and counter-intelligence. Could you look at tab 13 of the documentation that you were taken through by Mr. Cayley, please. We are early on in the story, the 28th of April, Mr. Crosland, and the summary of this DipTel speaks for itself. I just want to look at paragraph 4 with you, if I may. This is a briefing, I think, is it not, involving Colonel General Dimitrijevic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is as it were the report of the Colonel General speaking, and it's the last sentence which I'm putting under the head of intelligence I want to ask you about. "He added that the FRY security service had identified a training camp. They had the names of some 2 to 2.500 men who had been trained at the camp." First question, Mr. Crosland. Were you ever shown a list of the names yourself?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not shown a list of the names, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this claim that has a legitimacy as far as you're concerned? That is to say, the ability of the FRY security service to gather such a large number of names.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not actually at this particular incident as the paragraph makes clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had had other conversations with General Dimitrijevic who had indicated to me that they had a reasonable handle, in military terminology, on the activities going on on the other side of the border.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would your assessment be that they also had a reasonable handle on military activities going on against them within the borders? That is to say, what was your take on the abilities of the FRY security services to gather reliable information in your time there.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Electronic warfare capability was very reasonable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very reasonable.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And leading on from that you'll say, well, why didn't they use it -- did they not use it in a much better way. And that is a question that I have asked many people, including Mr. Milosevic, when I was in front of him last year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know, I've read it. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I don't know the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But they were capable and sophisticated intelligence-gathering people, FRY, on your assessment of them. Would that be fair? What they did with it is another matter, Mr. Crosland. I'm only concerned with their capability.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without downgrading the Albanian capability, I think at that particular time their electronic and wireless ability was probably not as sophisticated and, therefore, the Serbs with their more sophisticated sets did have the upper hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I want to deal with another aspect under the general head of intelligence and counter-intelligence, if I may please. Were you aware or did you become aware of the use by -- I'll use the term generally the Serb forces, you understand what I mean, Mr. Crosland, shorthand. Did you become aware of the use of infiltrators into the ranks of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think General Dimitrijevic did mention that on one occasion, yes. I can't specifically recall it, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it is an obvious line of --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is obvious, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for pre-empting me. What about something rather more than simple infiltration? That is to say, agent provocateur. You, of course, appreciate the slight difference. What about the use of them?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never privy to that type of information, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. I won't waste your time. What I think you were privy to is because you saw it was the arming of apparent civilians by the Serbs, were you not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've mention that to the Court on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You used the word "thugs" yesterday on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps I can expand on that. The various towns that were in that particular report mainly from Montenegro, the border towns close to that, Novi Pazar, Cetinje, Podgorica, et cetera, et cetera, this is one of the ways that elements of sometimes special police in civilian clothes, at other times paramilitaries, if we use that phrase, would move around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. When -- I don't ask you to turn it up. We'll remember it, I'm sure, from yesterday. Behind tab 7 is a detailed attempt at a Serbian security force analysis as of March 1998, and under the heading of "Outline of forces," show of overwhelming force, regarding the outer ring, there's talk of a capability of deploying up to 10.000 MUP for urban deployment, crowd control, assisted by imported thugs. Where were the thugs being imported from, Mr. Crosland? Were you aware?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were the gentlemen I'm was talking about just now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Were you aware of the functioning of the office of state security?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked a particular name, I think, in your final of three statements to this Tribunal, a David Gajic, and you indicated you did not know that gentleman. I wonder if I may put another name to you, Dragan Jasevic. Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name is not...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Familiar?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan is a very common name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But Jasevic may not be. He was the head of the office of state security responsible, if I'm rightly remember, for political delinquency?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take your word for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No dealings?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you have had any dealings --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not accredited to -- as I indicated first off, I was accredited purely to the Vojska Jugoslavije.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In a report that we in fact don't have in our bundles but it is a report in fact dated the 3rd -- I'm sorry, the report is dated the 5th of June. If anyone wants to cross-reference it in the Exhibits, it's R0428576 and onward. You haven't got did in front of you, Mr. Crosland, and I don't think you're going to need it. It's an analysis in June of 1998, as I say. It speaks about being in the area around Komorane, which was being still very tense, and it relates to - and you may remember this if you were there - a journey back to Pristina when people visited the civil military air field. There were 15 MiG jets in two rows on the air field, which had been flying training combat air patrol missions over Pristina during dusk and early evening. Now, do you remember this? Were you there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can recall in the early part of the -- this conflict that the Vojska Jugoslavije air force did -- did fly some training missions around Pristina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they have the use of helicopters?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Vojska Jugoslavije had a few number of helicopters. I came across, I think, one up towards Mitrovica. There were reports that helicopters had been used to assault various villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could never -- excuse me, I lost the word. Verify. Thank you. Verify or confirm these reports because by the time you started to talk to people who had been under bombardment of whatever kind, the stories would grow larger as fishermen do with fish.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's the last line of this report that I want to ask you about. The author says that this overflying combat air patrols, although training, is not new to Kosovo. It is more likely to be a rather unsubtle piece of psych ops. Psychological operation, is that what that's for?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a reasonable assessment, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you help us, please. What other kind of psych ops were the Serbian forces carrying out in the period of time we are interested in, Mr. Crosland, if you're aware of any?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suspect they used the communication networks to try and broadcast to the Albanian population which would be a perfectly reasonable tool to use.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: And by their actions alone, you could understand that they would -- we were putting a psychological fear --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- into the inhabitants of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I commented on this to the General Staff as a derogatory way of use of force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I turn then to -- away from intelligence to just one or two questions about the KLA. I don't know if the Court's going to have another break. Your Honour was looking at me in a meaningful way. I don't know whether that was meaning to indicate a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We would break now if you think that would be more convenient.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm entirely in the Court's hands. Mr. Crosland may welcome a break. Perhaps the interpreters might. I can indicate that I'm certainly I'm going to finish before the end of the session today given the -- I hope the lack of duplication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have a break now, resuming at ten minutes to. There's a reason for a slightly longer than usual break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Crosland, it's my fault, not yours. Could both you and I remember to pause after my question --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- and your answer to assist the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm told there is no Albanian translation. There is now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We were on the KLA, Mr. Crosland. Could I ask you this, please: Were you aware of armed Albanians engaged in fighting who were not members of the KLA but any other organisation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, as I indicated in Malisevo there were other nationalities who made their nationalities avail to be me. As far as I know, that's the only the time I saw people outside the Albanian population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to be clear, my question was specifically regarding Albanians. You were not aware of any other military or quasi-military organisation that was engaged in fighting at the time other than the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I was not aware of anyone, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to take you, if I may, to a passage in your second statement, Mr. Crosland, and I wanted to assist you whether Mr. Crosland could be given a copy of it, please. I know Mr. Hasan has copies available. I hope I'm not stealing Mr. Cayley's. Mr. Crosland, would you be good enough, please, to identify this as one of your three statements to the Tribunal? You will see the date towards the bottom of the first page. 7th December, 2000.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I ask you, please, to go to the third of 11 pages. Paragraph 9, first of all. "Based on my dealings with the KLA and knowledge of many of their operations, I do not think that its General Staff have particularly effective control over the organisation. The more committed and fervent KLA zone commanders conducted operations in their areas without any apparent sense of commitment to a higher command." And then a name: "Ramus Haradinaj," "Remi and Drini were particularly strong and independently-minded KLA regional commanders." For the future -- is that a characterisation of the totality of your dealings with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is a comment which as you read out I would agree with, yeah, at that particular time, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I can take you to the last two sentences or three of the same paragraph on the next page and I want you to if you can confirm that this is indeed the position. "I am unaware of the existence of any written KLA doctrine or of the ability of the organisation to impose discipline, especially that related to criminal acts and their prevention, nor am I aware of whether or not KLA commanders ever ordered criminal attacks." Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is -- that is the comment I made at the time and -- yes. I think that's a true comment, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I move on, then, to Lapusnik itself. Mr. Crosland, would it be any use pressing you on how many occasions between March and July you were in or around that village?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say there were many occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes we were allowed in, sometimes we were not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were allowed in, may I ask you this, were you introduced to or did you meet any KLA soldiers there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met some soldiers there, yes, who appeared to be on patrol in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's a grand way of putting it, I suppose, but I'm sure you'll get the effect of my question. Were you shown deployment of KLA forces in the village?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were some very obvious slit trenches that were local defensive positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were they located at various positions around the village?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, and up on the surrounding ridges adjacent to that particular village, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On subsequent occasions of your visits, did you meet the same or different KLA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I think it would be very difficult to say truthfully yes or no, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can, of course, meet people and never know their names or anything else other than their appearance. I mean, do you have any recollection now, and I know it's difficult these years later, meeting the same person more than once?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not particularly in this location, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware and can you help Their Honours with the deployment of Serb forces around Lapusnik at any stage?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The major position was at Komorane. It was a -- mainly a MUP position with various other elements in there as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it have the capacity to shell the village, the Serb forces, from outside of it when you saw their deployment?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall -- yes. Later on there was a VJ position there which had artillery, yes, to the south, to the south-east, I think it was, on a hill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Crosland, I recognised difficulty, but can you help us at all as to when that might have been, at least what month that was?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it may be from July or September, that period of time, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What we're given to understand is that Lapusnik, as the KLA no doubt would have put it fell to the Serb forces certainly on the 28th of July, and you were there, were you not, in that area on that very day witnessing what was undoubtedly the amassing of Serb forces. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've answered very clearly, if I may say so, Mr. Mansfield's questions regarding a camp or whatever in the Lapusnik itself. The reference to a prison camp at Glogovac, you'll recollect that, Mr. Mr. Crosland. It's just to remind you, if you want to look it up again, behind tab 20 of your exhibits --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- is the relevant telegram, where in paragraph 8, halfway through under "Security," it says there is talk of a KLA camp in Glogovac, impossible to substantiate. Did you ever go to a place that could be described as a prison camp?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is in Glogovac an industrial area that may -- could have been used as a prison camp. We had discussions later on that the Serbian security forces were using it as a prison camp. When I attempted to go into that area, quite naturally I was not allowed access for whatever reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't ask you to turn it up because I don't want to trouble you with too many documents, but at paragraph 21 of your second witness statement, in fact I think actually the statement you have in front of you, at 21 you say, if you're referring to the same place, Glogovac factory was used by the MUP and was obviously a place where suspicious activities took place, but I was never allowed into it."

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now that I've shown you that, do you wreck next that's putting it slightly higher, isn't it, obviously a place where suspicious activity took place?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I indicated to the Court, the security forces were extremely jumpy about me coming anywhere near it, so one can draw conclusions from that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to leave this subject of Lapusnik/camp in this way, Mr. Crosland, that until this case and your involvement in it as a witness, you were not personally aware of the allegation of the existence of the camp in Lapusnik? Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a fair comment, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I ask you, then, as a final heading, and I hope it can be fairly brief one, some general questions, tapping into your experiences there. First of all, this: We have heard very early on in this trial from a diplomat, a Mr. Kickert to be exact, of what he described as a tension between the KLA and the political party the LDK. Were you conscious of such tensions in Kosovo at the relevant time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was political comment by those following the political side that there appeared to be some tension between those two elements. As you are well aware, my job was to follow the military part, but it is integral that there is a military and political wing of a fledgling party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly. Can I ask you about the subject of imprisonment itself and invite you to consider this, Mr. Crosland: Given the situation as you regularly saw it, given the nature of the insurgency, given the nature of the Serb response, those three givens, activities by the insurgents whereby individuals are stopped, questioned, arrested, detained, imprisoned would all be of themselves typical of such a military situation, would they not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were typical of this particular military situation, yes. I wouldn't say every military situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course not. But Mr. Mansfield was asking you quite a bit about the north of Ireland. There it occurred, did it not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did. I would take great exception if people are inferring that Northern Ireland and the actions of the British army were in anyway linked to the actions of the KLA and the Serbian forces in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd take very strong objection to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Crosland, as it happens, nothing was further from my mind.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm very glad to hear it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think finally this: You'll recollect, no doubt, giving evidence in the trial of Milosevic. Mr. Crosland, you recollect --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes. Beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wonder if I might read to you - and we have distributed copies of it, it's only a paragraph - from page 8013 of the transcript of that trial.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the bottom of 8013 is a question from Mr. Milosevic himself, I think. It is: "Is it uncontested that the objectives of the attack or the targets were members of the Ministry of Interior, members of the military, civilians as well, Serbs, and Albanians, Muslims and members of other ethnic communities?" This is a general question regarding 1998. Mr. Milosevic goes on: "They were killed, they were kidnapped, they were robbed. Do you know about that? Did you know about that?" May I just read out your reply and ask you if it is something you stand by today, Mr. Crosland: "Yes, Mr. Milosevic, I knew about that. You must bear that in context with what your security forces were doing, something like 2 to 3 to 400 villages I saw burnt to the ground. It's not unnatural that people took revenge. I'm afraid reconciliation in the Balkans is not a word that's very much known about "osveta." More "osveta" and less -- a bit more "pomirenje" and less "osveta" would be a better thing all around. More reconciliation and less revenge." Do you stand by that, Mr. Crosland?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I stand by that, and I think I've indicated that throughout my current tour in the court. I would also, if I may, just go back to the previous point. When I went back into Kosovo after the conflict, I went to the prison at Istok, Dubrava, it's in the western part of Kosovo, up here to the north-east of Pec, and it was myself and one or two others who uncovered a whole mass of evidence that indicated orders for execution of various Albanian people. So I would hope that both things are taken in context, that one was trying to report firmly and fairly on what was a pretty nasty incident all round. So I would just like that to be added, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It has been -- it has been recorded, Mr. Crosland, and for my part I thank you for your patience and all the assistance you've given. I'm very grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Topolski. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Very few, Your Honour. Re-examined by Mr. Cayley:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Crosland, you'll be pleased to hear that you will actually be going home today rather than having to come back on Monday because I have very little. The Judges may have some questions for you. You made a comment in response to a question by Mr. Topolski a moment ago, and I'll read out your response that you said that you would take great exception if the actions of the British army were in any way linked to the actions of the KLA and Serbia in Kosovo. How were the actions of the KLA and the Serbs in Kosovo different from the actions of the British army in Northern Ireland?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't even put the two in the same sentence, frankly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you expand on why -- how operations were conducted? What was the distinction between the manner in which operations were conducted? I know it's obvious to you, but if you could explain to the Court the distinctions between the operations of the KLA and the Serbs in Kosovo and the operations of the British army in Northern Ireland?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there's any -- any connection whatsoever. The operations from the British army in Northern Ireland were carried out under a mandate that was legally applied to. Yes, there were mistakes made, as we all understand and appreciate. But to -- in any shape or form, to put these two operations together, I would not countenance any conversation on them, full stop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were operations carried out by the KLA and Serbs in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we've just had talked about with the Defence counsel, there was a great deal of room for retaliation because of the very heavy-handed nature of the Serbian operations. This does not immediately allow people to carry out counter-operations. But within the Balkans, this is the way people carry out their dealings. It's rather brutal, and I think we're all aware of that. And one tried, as I've said here, to report on -- on both sides accurately, fairly, and firmly, and to point out to the relevant people, and in my case to Vojska Jugoslavije, that certain actions that they were carrying out would do nothing to sort out this mess, which is still, as we know, ongoing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You responded earlier on actually to a question from Mr. Mansfield and it was about your characterisation of the KLA as a force, and you made the comment, and I copied it down. "The KLA made their mark in various ways. They gave a good account of themselves all the way through." What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a potentially lightly armed force, and certainly in the early part of 1998, as I've said already to the Court, they learned their lesson not to stand and fight but to use what we call the shoot-and-scoot tactics. And these they carried out with reasonable success as the Serbian casualties are quite clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Crosland.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I don't have any other questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cayley. I am pleased to be able to indicate that that concludes your evidence and you're free to return to your other activities. We would like to thank you for the assistance that you've given the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If there is no matter, it would seem a practical course to adjourn now for the weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will therefore adjourn. It has been pointed out, Mr. Cayley -- if you wouldn't mind just waiting there for a moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Have they been tendered?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No. I apologise. Mr. Younis did remind me. Could I, for simplicity, admit it as one exhibit because the map is actually at tab 1. So it would be tabs 1 to 42 inclusive, the Prosecutor's exhibit. I don't know what the next number is.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: You don't want the number individually assigned to each tab or just one number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: One exhibit number to the whole folder.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So that will be P92 for the full binder, including tab 1 to tab 42.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if it could be placed under seal, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Exhibit P92 will be admitted, being a binder of documents, and they will be under seal. That being so, we will now adjourn until 2.15 on Monday. Oh, 4.00 on Monday, as another Trial Chamber has to use this court to deliver a decision at 2.15. So we are delayed, I am afraid, until 4.00. Until Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 17th day of January, 2005, at 4.00 p.m. 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.20 p.m.,
